rv.q: The whole is electrifying, with a consistent emotional intensity.

With her immensely vivid stage presence, Gayle, aka pioneering reggae artist Lorna Gee, draws us through the memories that rise and subside as she recalls her life and the forces that have shaped her.
Gayle’s otherworldly presence is hard to look away from.
It is intriguing, gripping and frustratingly bitty.
The Legends of Them is a lingering, thought-provoking, beautifully produced piece that defies easy definition but works immaculately, entirely on its own terms.
This is a thoroughly entertaining and thought-provoking piece of theatre.
The Legends of Them is nothing short of awe-inspiring.
At its best this gig is an example of subtle storytelling and alluring music.

Particularly impressive is Joshie Harriette’s evocative lighting design, taking full advantage of a large rig upstage centre to grab our attention at certain times. Sutara plays not only herself but also the ‘legends’ plus more than twenty-five other characters.
She manoeuvres every movement, teasing her audience with great humour and exposing her own trauma in front of us like a sharp scalpel.
While a tragic story of a family, it ends positively and the audience appear to have their expectations fulfilled.
Lorna Gee created an inspiring, moving and vibrant show in which she obviously put her whole heart in with great generosity.

cn.t: Reggae pioneer Sutara Gayle's autobiographical journey earns mostly positive reviews for its vivid storytelling and powerful stage presence, though some find the elliptical structure challenging. Critics praise the blend of music, memory, and personal history.
